extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, social theory, and humour studies
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying sociological criteria for analyzing humour, laughter, ridicule and embarrassment in social interaction, with attention to function, consequences, and social order. Suited to academic analysis or teaching in social theory/humour studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as a rhetorical device (not exclusive to radicals)
rubrics_metrics.description: If laughter is rhetorical, then it can no more be the property of radicals than any other type of rhetorical device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat laughter as a rhetorical resource available to any social actor; do not assume that rebellious-seeming laughter automatically indexes progressive or anti-bigoted positions. Evaluate who uses laughter and how they rhetorically position it (e.g. as rebellious) rather than assuming the stance of the laugher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bigotry and humour can be integrally connected (Sartre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bigotry resembled a joke, because bigots do not, indeed cannot, really believe in the literal truth of their outrageously expressed opinions and grossly exaggerated stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether humour functions to mock standards of liberalism and tolerance while simultaneously enabling bigots to 'free' themselves from rational or moral constraint. Examples: racist jokes by Ku Klux Klan members; extremist jokes that revel in offensiveness (torture, lynching). Consider that offensive humour can communicate a serious ideological message even when framed as jest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish psychological nature from sociological consequences (motive ≠ effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some acts of humour might appear rebellious to participants, but the consequences of such humour might be conformist rather than radical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humour, separately consider (a) participants' subjective experience or claimed motive (feeling rebellious) and (b) the actual social consequences (disciplinary, conservative, reinforcing power). Examples: backstage practical jokes that teach apprentices their place; Gillray cartoons enjoyed by the well-born without subverting their status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical jokes often discipline and humiliate (teach lessons)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical joke may well appear to participants as 'just a joke'... But there is no actual rebellion in these jokes... By teaching the apprentice a lesson that will not be forgotten easily, the professionals are strengthening the codes that maintain the structure of differential power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate practical jokes for their humiliation function and pedagogic/disciplinal outcome. Examples provided: returning a dropped handkerchief at arm's length; the Tommy Simpson lavatory joke. Consider both immediate enjoyment and the longer-term lesson enforced on the victim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebellious humour can have conservative/disciplinary functions
rubrics_metrics.description: At times, rebellious humour – or humour that is claimed and experienced as rebellious – can have conservative and disciplinary functions; the enjoyment of mass-marketed rebellious humour directly aids the economic structures that have produced such enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether humour that claims to subvert actually reinforces authority, economic systems, or social order (e.g., mass-market 'naughty' humour that integrates consumers into capitalism). Use historical examples (goliards, Gillray) and theoretical account (Zijderveld) showing mockery can reaffirm the power of authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whispered jokes as alibis/self-persuasion under repression
rubrics_metrics.description: The whispered jokes that are circulated in totalitarian regimes are not actually rebellious. Instead, they provide alibis for those who do not dare to rebel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing humour in authoritarian contexts, consider whether jokes function as safety-valves of conscience (self-persuasion) rather than as catalysts for political change. Example: soldiers or citizens telling jokes about commanders/dictators but continuing to obey; jokes enable people to 'feel' rebellious without acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral framing/self-persuasion matters more than the moment of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment of humour itself is not what counts — what counts is what one believes to be the moral point of one's laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the interpretive framing audiences or tellers attach to humour (e.g., 'I was just joking', 'we were being naughty') because this belief can function to protect social order by convincing actors (and themselves) that they are morally acceptable or rebellious when they are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and markers of embarrassment (Goffman)
rubrics_metrics.description: The signs include blushing, fumbling, sweating, breaking of the voice, etc.; embarrassment is a feeling of discomfiture that 'seems always to be unpleasant'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these observable signs to identify embarrassment in interactional analysis. Remember embarrassment typically occurs publicly (in front of an audience) and is tied to 'unfulfilled expectations' or breaches of interactional codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embarrassment is situational and distinct from shame
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassment is much more temporary and tied to particular situations, whereas shame involves a general and enduring sense that the self is unworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate embarrassment (short-lived, public, linked to specific interactional gaffes) from shame (longer-lasting, private or global self-evaluation) when assessing emotional consequences of humour or social breaches. Note Scheff's characterization of embarrassment as a less intense form of shame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face-work and social codes maintain social order
rubrics_metrics.description: Much interaction is structured around the need for social actors to present themselves acceptably to others and, thereby, to 'maintain face'. Threats to face can be threats to social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse humour in relation to face-saving strategies and the micro-rules of interaction (politeness norms, turn-taking, adjacency pairs). Consider how humour either threatens face (causing embarrassment) or is used to repair/save face (e.g., apologies, jocular mitigation). Examples: indirect requests ('Please could you pass the salt?'), repeated 'No comment' as a response to interrogation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of embarrassing situations: faux pas, sticky situations, centre of attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Sabini et al. suggest three main types of embarrassing situation: faux pas (failed negotiation of routine interaction), sticky situations (things turning out wrong, discrediting another's performance), and being the centre of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify episodes of humour/embarrassment using these categories to predict likely reactions and functions. For instance, faux pas typically arise from breaches of routine etiquette; sticky situations involve unexpected, awkward presences (ex-partners); centre-of-attention problems have distinct dynamics from the other two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joking can relieve tension and deny conflicting reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Joking and joshing undermine the seriousness of the conflicting situation in which the participants find themselves... it is natural, then, to find embarrassment and joking going together, for both help in denying the same reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing interactional moments of tension (e.g., manager/worker in egalitarian context), consider whether humour functions as a tension-relief mechanism that restores interactional smoothness by 'denying' or reframing the conflict. Use Goffman's observation that joshing can be a mutually-recognized tactic to manage awkward role conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour and social 'seriousness' are co-constructed
rubrics_metrics.description: The two phenomena – the seriousness of the social world and its comedy – may be integrally connected; a social theory of humour requires a social theory of seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In broader analyses, situate specific humorous acts within the larger social construction of reality: shared codes, language stability, and the perceived 'out-there-ness' of what is funny. Evaluate whether humour is operating against, within, or to reproduce the taken-for-granted serious order.
